bundle.name: Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong: eight days worth cloning
bundle.description: Palace mornings and market crawls in Seoul, a Busan day that ends on the sand, a Taipei day that starts in a hot spring, the two Taiwanese days that need a driver and a 4am train, and Hong Kong twice — once for six dollars, once for two thousand.
sources: PROVENANCE: written without live web access (the session's search budget was spent and outbound fetches were blocked), so venue names, prices and opening rules come from model knowledge rather than pages read at authoring time. The URLs below are canonical references for those facts, NOT sources that were fetched and checked. Treat every price and time here as needing a verification pass before it is quoted as fact — see KI-2026-09-06-d.

playbooks.name: Seoul: hanbok at the gate, two palaces, and Euljiro on plastic stools
playbooks.summary: The palace day done in the right order — rent the outfit first because it is what makes the gates free, then spend the afternoon in a 1920s hanok alley and the night on a stool in a tool-shop backstreet.

sourceTrip.name: Two weeks between Seoul and Taipei

stops.title: Rent the hanbok before anything else

location.name: Hanbok rental shops on Yulgok-ro, Gyeongbokgung side

stops.notes: Take the full-day rate (about 30,000 won), not the four-hour one — four hours runs out somewhere between the two palaces, and the hanbok is the thing that makes both gates free. Pick a proper full-length outfit; the novelty 'fusion' dresses get turned away at the ticket window as not counting. Most shops store your bag and pin your hair for a few thousand won more, which is worth it because you cannot carry a daypack in this.

stops.title: Gyeongbokgung from the 09:00 opening, then the guard change
stops.notes: Closed Tuesdays, and that one fact breaks the entire day — check the weekday before you plan anything else. Entry is 3,000 won, or free in hanbok, which is the whole reason the rental comes first. At the opening bell walk hard LEFT to Gyeonghoeru and the Hyangwonjeong pond: every tour group turns right for the throne hall, and the water sits empty for twenty minutes. Then come back out to Gwanghwamun for the Sumunjang changing of the guard at 10:00 — it repeats at 14:00, and does not run on Tuesdays either.

stops.title: Bukchon, but the lanes nobody polices
stops.notes: Bukchon-ro 11-gil is the lane in every photograph and it is now a managed zone with posted visiting hours, marshals and residents who will absolutely tell you off — people live behind those doors and the signs asking for quiet are not decoration. Walk it once, quietly, then go uphill off Gyedong-gil instead: same rooftops, real neighbourhood, nobody counting heads.

stops.title: Lunch out of a brass tin at Tongin Market
stops.notes: Upstairs at the info counter you buy an empty brass lunch tin and ten brass yeopjeon coins for 5,000 won, then walk the aisle filling it a coin at a time — tteokbokki, jeon, fried things — and eat at the communal tables. The coin cafe is closed Mondays. Rice and soup are cash, not coins, which is the bit that trips everyone up at the first stall.

stops.title: Changdeokgung, and the Secret Garden ticket you must have already bought
stops.notes: Closed Mondays — which, with Gyeongbokgung shut on Tuesdays, means this day only works Wednesday to Sunday. Hanbok gets you into the palace free but NOT into Huwon: the Secret Garden is a separate 5,000 won timed, guided, capped ticket, and the English-language slots go first. Book it on the palace website up to six days ahead; the small same-day allocation at the gate is gone before 10:00.

stops.title: Ikseon-dong, one turn off the main strip
stops.notes: Jongno 3-ga exit 6 drops you at the mouth of it. This was a 1920s speculative hanok estate built as cheap housing, which is why the alleys are barely shoulder-width — at weekends they move single file, so come on a weekday. Return the hanbok on the way in if your shop is a Jongno one. The courtyard tea houses one turn off the main lane cost half what the photographed ones on it do.

stops.title: Nogari and beer on a stool in Euljiro
stops.notes: Euljiro 3-ga exit 4, then the alley of plastic stools that materialises around 18:00 and is packed away by midnight. Manseon Hof is the original: dried pollack grilled over a burner at your table, gochujang mayo to dip, and beer that costs less than the fish. You sit outdoors in any weather — in January they hand out blankets and nobody moves inside.

stops.title: A bar behind an unmarked door
stops.notes: The joke of Euljiro is that the good bars are on the third floor of tile-and-tool wholesale buildings, up a freight lift that looks decommissioned, behind a door with no sign. Nothing is findable by map pin and that is deliberate. Ask the table next to you at the nogari alley which building, then take the lift to whichever floor the noise is coming from.

playbooks.name: Seoul: Gwangjang at eleven, a jjimjilbang at noon, a three-star counter at eight
playbooks.summary: The cheapest and the most expensive meals in the city, ten hours apart, with four hours of hot rooms and cold plunges in between so you arrive at dinner boiled clean and starving.

stops.title: Gwangjang Market: bindaetteok, mayak gimbap, yukhoe, in that order
stops.notes: Jongno 5-ga exit 8, on a weekday before noon — many stalls take Sunday off and the whole place is unusable after 18:00. The central aisle nearest the exit is the tourist gauntlet; the yukhoe alley on the north side is where Seoul actually eats, and raw beef with a raw egg yolk and sesame oil at 11am is better than it sounds. Ask the price and check the posted board before you sit: the market got publicly hammered in 2024 for short-weighing tourists, and prices are now displayed precisely so you can point at them. One mung bean pancake feeds two. Cash or a Korean transfer.

stops.title: Line 1 down to Yongsan
stops.notes: Straight down Line 1, no changes, about fifteen minutes. Buy a T-money card at any convenience store for 3,000 won and load it there — transfers inside 30 minutes are free, and it also pays for buses, taxis and half the vending machines. Contactless foreign cards still do not work on the Seoul metro gates.

stops.title: Four hours at Dragon Hill Spa
stops.notes: Out of Yongsan station, cross the plaza, it is the enormous pagoda-looking thing — open 24 hours, about 17,000 won for a day pass. The wristband they give you is your locker key and your tab: everything inside is charged to it and you settle on the way out. Rules that matter: shower and scrub thoroughly before you get into any tub, the bathing floors are nude and single-sex, the cotton shorts and tee are the uniform for the mixed floors upstairs, and no swimsuits anywhere. Baked eggs and a cold sikhye in the salt room is the canonical order. Tattoos are not an issue here, which is not true of every jjimjilbang.

stops.title: Leeum, because the permanent collection is free
stops.notes: Closed Mondays. The permanent collection — the celadon and the Joseon painting in the Mario Botta rotunda — has been free since 2021, but you still need to reserve a timed slot on their site, and evening slots go last so book that morning. It is a genuinely steep ten minutes uphill from Hangang-jin exit 1, and it puts you a five-minute walk from dinner.

stops.title: The counter at Mosu Seoul
stops.notes: One seating, one menu, and the reservation is the hard part: bookings open on CatchTable at the start of the month for the following month and are gone in minutes, so set an alarm rather than trying your luck. Ask for the counter, not the room — the whole point is watching it happen. Wine pairing roughly doubles the bill; the non-alcoholic pairing here is not a consolation prize. Smart casual, no shorts, and do not be late for a fixed seating.

stops.title: A last drink in Gangnam
stops.notes: A zero-waste cocktail bar that keeps landing on the Asia's 50 Best list, which means walk-ins queue. Message them for a table when you book dinner and hold it loosely — after a three-hour tasting menu there is a real chance you would rather go to bed, and this is the stop to drop without guilt.

playbooks.name: Busan: Gamcheon in the morning light, Jagalchi at lunch, Gwangalli after dark
playbooks.summary: A pork soup breakfast, a hillside of painted houses before the queues, a fish you choose downstairs and eat upstairs, and raw fish carried out to a table facing a lit bridge.

stops.title: Dwaeji gukbap in the Seomyeon soup alley
stops.notes: Busan's own dish and its breakfast: milky pork bone broth, rice, and a plate of raw chives and salted shrimp you tip in yourself, a spoonful at a time, tasting as you go — it arrives deliberately underseasoned and salting it at the table is the whole ritual. Order 'sooyuk baekban' if you want the pork served separately on a plate rather than in the bowl. The old shops behind Seomyeon Market open at 07:00 and are busiest with people going to work, which is the right time to be there.

stops.title: Line 1 to Toseong, then the little green bus 2
stops.notes: Exit 6, walk up past the hospital, and take the small green village bus 2 or 2-2 from the stop on the hill — it grinds up the switchbacks in ten minutes. Walking it is twenty-five minutes of stairs for no reward. Your T-money card from Seoul works on Busan buses and the metro.

stops.title: Gamcheon Culture Village before the coach parties
stops.notes: Buy the 2,000 won stamp map at the information centre at the top — it is the only way to make sense of the lanes, and the stamps get you a printed photo at the end. Do the Little Prince statue first: the queue for that bench is over half an hour by 11:00 and non-existent at 09:45. Then abandon the marked route and walk the back lanes downhill. This is a real neighbourhood built by refugees in the 1950s; the alleys shaded red on the map are private front doors, not a shortcut.

stops.title: Pick it downstairs, eat it upstairs at Jagalchi
stops.notes: Closed the first and third Tuesday of the month — the single thing that ruins this day. The system: choose your fish from a tank on the ground floor, agree the price BEFORE it comes out of the water, then carry it upstairs where a restaurant charges a per-person cooking fee (around 10,000 won) for the banchan, the sesame leaves and the maeuntang they make from the frame afterwards. Every upstairs room charges roughly the same, so pick the one with locals in it. Flatfish and abalone are the safe order; the live octopus is a texture decision, not a flavour one.

stops.title: Seed-stuffed hotteok at BIFF Square
stops.notes: Ssiat hotteok is a Busan invention and the stall to join is simply the one with the queue at the Nampo end of BIFF Square: they fry the sugar-filled pancake, snip it open with scissors and shovel in sunflower and pumpkin seeds. Eat it standing, out of the paper cup, and do not bite straight in — the molten sugar inside is a genuine hazard. Gukje Market behind it is where to spend the next twenty minutes.

stops.title: The cliff path at Huinnyeoul on Yeongdo
stops.notes: Bus 6 or 71 over the bridge from Nampo, twenty minutes. It is the quiet version of Gamcheon — the same tin-roofed refugee housing, but on a cliff above the shipping lane, with a path at sea level below it. Drop this stop without regret if Jagalchi ran long; it exists so the afternoon has somewhere to go.

stops.title: Buy the fish downstairs at Millak, eat it facing the bridge
stops.notes: Not a restaurant — a building of fishmongers. Buy hoe by the kilo on the ground floor, pay a small per-head seating charge upstairs, and they plate it for you at a table with the whole of Gwangan Bridge in the window. Bring soju and beer from the convenience store next door; that is expected here and nowhere else. Go up to the terrace level rather than taking the first table offered.

stops.title: Gwangalli beach while the bridge is lit
stops.notes: The bridge is lit nightly and the sand is a legal drinking area, so half of Busan is sitting on it with a tent and a chicken box. On Saturday nights there is usually a drone light show over the water — check the Suyeong-gu schedule, because on those nights the beach fills an hour beforehand and the surf-shop end near Millak is the only place left with a sightline.

playbooks.name: Taipei: a Beitou soak, Yongkang lunch, Elephant Mountain at dusk, Raohe at night
playbooks.summary: Sulphur at nine, soup dumplings at noon, the skyline at golden hour from a staircase, and a pepper bun straight out of a clay oven — one MRT card, about thirty-five dollars.

sourceTrip.name: Taiwan, north to south and back

stops.title: Red line to Beitou, change onto the two-carriage branch
stops.notes: Xinbeitou is not on the main red line — get off at Beitou and cross the platform to the little two-car shuttle that runs one stop up the valley; one of its carriages is fitted out as a hot-spring themed train. Buy an EasyCard at any MTR customer service window for NT$100 and top it up at any 7-Eleven: it pays for the metro, buses, the gondola, lockers and most convenience stores, and it gives you a fare discount over single tickets.

stops.title: The Millennium public hot spring
stops.notes: About NT$60 and it is a public bath, not a private onsen: swimsuit AND swim cap are compulsory, and they sell neither cheaply at the door, so bring both. It runs in timed sessions with the pools cleared and refilled between them, so arrive at the start of one rather than halfway through. The terraces step downhill from hottest to coldest — start at the bottom, because the top pool is genuinely 42-45C and people misjudge it. Lockers take coins.

stops.title: Ten minutes at the Thermal Valley
stops.notes: Free, closed Mondays, and honestly ten minutes long — a jade-green sulphur lake steaming at about 90C, which is why nobody bathes in it and why the bathhouses downhill have water at all. Worth the detour only because it is four minutes' walk from the baths you have just left.

stops.title: Xiaolongbao on Yongkang Street, the sensible way
stops.notes: Dongmen station exit 5 puts you at the top of the street. The Din Tai Fung every guidebook sends you to — the original on Xinyi Road — closed in 2024, so stop looking for it: the Taipei 101 mall branch is the reliable one and it issues queue numbers through its app, so take a number from the MRT and arrive when it is nearly up. If the wait is still absurd, Kao Chi on Yongkang itself does an equally good soup dumpling plus a shengjianbao and a Shanghainese rice cake that nobody queues for, and Yongkang Beef Noodle two minutes away is the other correct answer to lunch here.

stops.title: Mango shaved ice, if it is the season
stops.notes: Only worth the queue between roughly May and September, when the mango on top is fresh Irwin fruit from the south. Out of season the same NT$220 buys frozen puree on shaved milk ice and the whole thing collapses into sweetness — order the taro or peanut version instead, which is what the ice shops are actually good at year-round.

stops.title: The guard change on the plaza at Chiang Kai-shek Memorial
stops.notes: One MRT stop from Dongmen and free. The honour guard ceremony is hourly on the hour and now takes place out on the plaza rather than upstairs under the statue, which means you can actually see it and there is shade at the edges. Stand on the north side so the arch is behind them. The exhibition in the basement about how the building's own meaning has been fought over since 2017 is more interesting than the hall above it.

stops.title: Elephant Mountain, 45 minutes before the sun goes
stops.notes: Xiangshan station exit 2, then about fifteen minutes of steep concrete stairs. Forty-five minutes before sunset is the number that matters: the Six Giant Rocks — the boulders everyone stands on to frame Taipei 101 — hold maybe twenty people, and they are all taken by golden hour. Get there early, claim a rock, wait. Carry water and a head torch: the handrail lighting on the way down is patchy and the stairs are slick after rain. If the rocks are full, keep climbing five more minutes to the photographer's platform above them.

stops.title: Raohe Street, entering at the temple end
stops.notes: Songshan station exit 5 puts you at the Ciyou Temple gate, which is the end you want: the black pepper bun stall is the first thing on the right and the queue moves fast because they come out of a clay tandoor in batches. Wait five minutes before biting one — the pork and spring onion inside is molten. Then walk the middle third for the medicinal spare rib soup and the taro balls, ignore the games and the phone cases, and turn round at the far gate rather than doubling the length. One straight street, no branches, so nobody gets lost.
